utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This is case number IT-01-47-T, Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel and to everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi and Daryl Mundis, assisted by our case manager Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Appearances for the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team, appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura for today, Rodney Dixon, assisted by Mr. Nermin Mulalic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On Monday, 31st January 2005, we resume with our hearing. If there are no issues to be raised, we are going to bring the witness into the courtroom, the witness that has been envisaged for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. First of all, let me see whether you can hear the interpretation of my words in English. If that is the case, can you please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear you very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a Defence witness, and before we ask you to take the solemn declaration, we would like to hear your name, your family name, the date of birth, the place of birth and your nationality.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: My name is Robert Alexander Stewart. I was born on the 7th of July, 1949. I'm British, and I was born in Preston, Lancashire, United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Currently are you employed? What is your position at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am director of global risks for Group 4 Securicor, Global Risks Limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, what was your position at the time when you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a lieutenant colonel. I commanded the 1st Battalion of the Cheshire Regiment. I was the British Battalion commander in Central Bosnia, Northern Bosnia, and Southern Bosnia, which was my operational area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified either before an international court or a national court with regard to the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or is this the first time you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not the first time I have testified. I have testified before the International Criminal Tribunal on at least two occasions before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that you have testified on two occasions. Could you please tell the Chamber in which cases have you testified and whether you have been called as a Prosecution witness or a Defence witness on those occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the case of Blaskic, I was called by the Judges. I can't remember in the case of Kordic, Santic, who called me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you now read the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Before I give the floor to the Defence team, I would like to provide you with certain explanation as to how the session will take place. Since you have already testified before the International Criminal Tribunal, you're familiar with the procedure. First of all, you are going to answer the questions put to you by the Defence lawyers of General Hadzihasanovic, whom you have already met with in preparation for your testimony. The Defence lawyers are going to put to you questions within the so-called examination-in-chief. Those questions must not be leading. In other words, they must not suggest certain answers to you. This will last about an hour and a half, and after that the Prosecution, on your right-hand side, will proceed with their cross-examination. The time that the Prosecution will have at their disposal is identical to the time used by the Defence. You already know that the questions that the Prosecution puts to you may be somewhat longer and more leading, and you will sometimes be able to answer them with a yes or no. After that stage, the Defence, if they so wish, will be allowed to ask you some additional questions that arise from the Prosecutor's questions. After that, the three Judges who are in front of you will take the time to put questions to you either to clarify the answers that you have given to one party or the other or because the Judges will want to clarify some of the things that remain vague in your answers. After that, both parties will be given an opportunity to put questions to you arising from the Judges' questions. The Defence will be given the floor last, and they will be allowed to put any questions to you in order to clarify the matters. This is in general terms how your testimony will develop. There are two more things that I would like to emphasise. First of all, you have taken the solemn declaration, which means that you should not give us false testimony, but this is in your case almost unnecessary. There is also another element that I have to inform you about. That is that at the moment when you are asked a question, if you believe that the answer may one day be used against you and incriminate you, you may refuse to answer. The Chamber may then compel you to provide your answer and guarantee you a form of immunity. You understand that this is a verbal procedure, and we don't have any documents. The two parties will have some documents to show you, but in any case, your words are very important. If you do not understand a question and if a question is too complicated for you to answer, you may always demand the party who has put it to you to rephrase it. Whatever problem you may encounter during your testimony, do not hesitate to ask for the Judges' assistance. Having said all this, I'm going to give the floor to the Defence who are going to start with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. We have had the opportunity of meeting before your testimony today and before this trial Chamber, but for the benefit of the transcript let me just -- allow me to introduce myself and the colleagues I'm working with today. That is Stephane Bourgon, counsel from Canada; Mrs. Edina Residovic, who is a counsel from Sarajevo; and Ms. Muriel Cauvin, who is our legal assistant. Together, as you know, we represent the accused General Hadzihasanovic, and my aim today is to ask you a few questions with respect to your deployment in Central Bosnia in 1993.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, 1992 I deployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1992. Sorry. And we will come back to that. Thank you very much for the correction, Colonel. Let me begin by simply saying that considering that we both speak the same language, we will try to speak slowly so that the interpreters can catch up with us for in simultaneous translation in both French and B/C/S. I have a tendency to speak very fast. The interpreters are probably already shaking because I am doing the witness today. I will try to go slowly and I would ask you to do the same. Colonel, how long have you been a member of the British Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I was a member of the British Armed Forces for 28 years; two years as an officer cadet and 26 years as an officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I have some information here that pertains to your career, and what I propose to do, with the consent of my colleague, is to simply lead you through your CV in order to save time. If I understand correctly, you are the son of an officer in the British Armed Forces. At 18 years old you attended the Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst, and at the age of 20, you were commissioned as an officer with a specific qualification of infantry officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, let me interrupt you. You can put that question to the witness. However, your questions are rather leading. We want to gain time, so theoretically we shouldn't allow you to do that, but we are concerned with the time. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We have certainly no objection to leading any of the background information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Go ahead, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is just about the curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Colonel, your first assignment as a platoon commander, as an infantry platoon commander was in Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the age of 24, the government decided to send you back to university to attend a degree in international politics and strategy, a degree that you completed with a first class degree.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then returned to the Sandhurst Military Academy as an instructor before attending the Army Staff College for a period of one year, which was the first possible year that you could attend such a high-level college.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: That is correct, except I was also in Northern Ireland several times in various positions in between that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And following your attendance at the Army Staff College, at 32 years old you were promoted major, and you became a company commander where again you were sent in various positions in Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I was a company commander in Northern Ireland for two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us a bit about your experience as a company commander in Northern Ireland, whether anything specific happened to you while you were there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. On the 6th of December, 1982, I had six men killed and 35 wounded in an operation carried out by the Irish National Liberation Army. It was a bomb. And that, in my view, was something that very much marks out those two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. If I understand, you were then posted or transferred to the Ministry of Defence where you worked in two military operations, one responsible for all deployments of the British army overseas before being assigned as second in command of your own battalion, the Cheshire, in Central America, where you went for six months?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct. I also guarded the Queen in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at 37 years old you were promoted to lieutenant colonel, which is a very young age to achieve this rank, and you were then assigned as the military assistant to the chairman of the NATO Military Committee where, amongst other things, you accomplished the duties of speech writer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, you were -- still as a lieutenant colonel, you, finally, achieved the dream of every military officer and that is of being assigned as commander of your own regiment, the Cheshire Regiment.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is in August 1992 that you were informed about your deployment to Central Bosnia where you deployed in September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I personally deployed in September. My battalion was a bit later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You returned from Bosnia in -- on the 12th of May, 1992. You were promoted to full colonel in 1994, and assigned as the chief policy in the supreme allied headquarters in Belgium.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Not correct. I was returned on -- I think it was the 11th or 12th of May, 1993, and I became chief of policy at supreme headquarters allied powers Europe in I think it was January 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I think that was my mistake. It's not a transcript mistake; I gave you the wrong information. And you finally retired from the British forces in 1996.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: January 1996; correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Let us now move to some of the highlights of what happened during your mission in Bosnia, and the first thing I would like to confirm with you: While you were in Bosnia, did you keep notes or did you maintain some type of a diary of your activities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I started a diary when General Sir Jeremy Mackenzie, my old boss, told me I had better do so because one day I may well be in a court of law having to say what had happened during my time in Bosnia, so I started it after my old colleague told me to start a diary. I did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, has this diary been used by yourself when you testified in previous trials, and do you have this diary with you today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: It was used by myself in previous trials, and I have it with me today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is quite possible that during the testimony I ask the permission of the Chamber for the witness to be allowed to refresh his memory by referring to his diary which he kept during his stay in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] In addition to publishing a diary, or at least maintaining your diary in Bosnia, did you also write a book on your experience in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I did, because the army told me to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we compare today the contents of your book with the contents of your diary, how would they be the same or differ?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I used the diary as the source for the book. Obviously a book should not be like a diary, so sometimes I group things together in my book, but really the source of what actually was happening was my diary, because I wrote that normally between 7.15 and 0730 the morning following the day before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber the steps that you took and the difficulties that you encountered in setting up the British contingent of UNPROFOR in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yeah, I can. It was an appalling task for a lieutenant colonel to be given, because the Ministry of Defence, to start with, gave me no mission whatsoever for three months, and everyone in this court will understand that a military officer without a mission is sometimes like a ship without a rudder. I deployed with a small group of people into the Balkans, not sure exactly which country we were to go to and make a plan, something like September, October of 1992. For two weeks we tried to find a way to get to Tuzla, having landed at Zagreb and borrowed some Land Rovers, and we drove into Serbia, and we went into Bosnia by the bridge at Zvornik. It was very difficult and quite dangerous, and we were blocked all the time. And I thank the United Nations from the bottom of my heart for expelling Serbia from the United Nations right at the time I was in the middle of Serbia wearing a blue beret. But seriously, it was quite difficult, and at the end of about a week, I went back to Zagreb via Banja Luka. I could not get to Tuzla from that direction, and in Banja Luka, I met Air Chief Marshal Sir Kenneth Hayr, who had flown in to see me and the other members of the team, and he said, "We've decided you're to try to get into Bosnia now from the south via Split. Take two aircraft now, take two Land Rovers, and go and do it." I asked the air chief marshal what he wanted me to achieve, and he said, "Try and find something that's a good plan."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. How much did you know about Central Bosnia and the area that you finally deployed into?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Practically nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much logistics did you have already in theatre when you deployed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: There was a British medical unit at Zagreb but no one anywhere near Bosnia, so none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you encounter any difficulties in getting your soldiers over?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that was much longer, much later, and by that time we had a good -- good enough plan. So by that time, no. But getting my reconnaissance team into Central Bosnia was extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if I would ask you to compare the difficulties that you encountered in setting up the British Battalion and the establishment of the 3rd Corps of the army in Bosnia and Herzegovina, could you help the Trial Chamber in this respect?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think I could have done it. To try and establish a 3rd Corps or any corps from nothing, with no real weapons, with no organisation, it must have been an impossible task. And I believed -- and I -- perhaps later you'll ask me again, but I believe the organisation of the 3rd Corps was extremely fluid in consequence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, did your organisation upon deployment have standard operating procedures, established doctrine, and a history on which to base its operations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Of course. We were a regular army of a country that's been in existence for a very long time, and standard operational procedures, weapons, logistics, were all set already, so at least I didn't have to worry about that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How well did you know your officers when you deployed in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I had been commanding the battalion for, I should think, about 18 months by that time, but I had always been an officer of the Cheshire Regiment, so I not only knew the officers below me, but I was serving with some of the sons of the sergeants when I first joined the regiment, so I knew the soldiers extremely well, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last two questions: How would that apply to the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I assume that the 3rd Corps was made up of people that were just brought together. It must have been extremely difficult. I understand, too, that the top people, you would try to get them from the old Yugoslav national army, but that didn't necessarily work either. Some people came from the navy, the Yugoslav navy, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would there be a difference, Colonel, between the British Battalion moving into a war zone as a neutral party if we try to compare this with the 3rd Corps, an army which was fighting for its survival?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: A huge difference. It's even more -- more difficult. If you're fighting for your survival and you have these problems, you have a practically impossible task, in my view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment, Colonel, on the rank structure within the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: It's a question I asked myself right from the start, not only the Bosnia-Herzegovina army but also the HVO as well. It was something I tried to set myself to find out what was happening. It seemed to me that the HVO did have some kind of rank structure, and I started to see ranks appearing on the officers' dress from November, December time, 1992. I never saw such rank in the BiH. I fundamentally just used to allocate titles rather arbitrarily. For example, General Hadzihasanovic, although I didn't necessarily think General Hadzihasanovic, as he is, of course, was a general appointed specifically by rank at that time. "Commander" was a way around this problem, to call someone a commander. It works at all levels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And early in time, Colonel, if we compare the HVO and the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, how would they compare?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: They were not like my -- my unit. The HVO had organisation. The HVO had weapons, equipment, and resources. The BiH had something but not very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: The HVO had a lot more, for example, artillery and even the odd tank, which I didn't really see much in evidence among the BiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, you set up the British Battalion. In order to avoid leading you, where did you set up the British Battalion in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: We found a school on the outskirts of Vitez, Your Honour. It was empty, so we were quite careful. We didn't want to get accusations that we had emptied a school of children. It was empty at the time and we made our base there. We found an empty factory at Gornji Vakuf, some two hours to the south, and we based ourselves on those two locations. And I wanted and I was instructed in the end to get to Tuzla, which was about another 180 kilometres north, where eventually I found the air field deserted and put a company location up there by the beginning of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, were there any strategic reasons why you chose Vitez and those other locations you spoke about, or was it simply a matter of logistics and availability?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: It was a mixture of everything. We initially wanted to be around Vitez because there was a United Nations High Commission for Refugees depot meant to be there, which opened up again when we were there. We were given -- kind of given an operational area that extended from Tuzla all the way down to Tomislavgrad, and so we tried to position ourselves in appropriate places to cover that sort of area. I only had at a maximum 900 men and some women, and it was -- we were quite stretched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, do you -- based on what you could experience in your relationship with both the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO, would you say that the HVO benefited from the fact that the British Battalion was located in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: They might have done. They were very helpful, particularly Blaskic helping us getting in there, and even Siljeg down in Tomislavgrad. They helped us get in. They guided us a little bit across the mountains. We talked to them. But equally I talked, as soon as I could, to the BiH and tried to speak to the Bosnian Serb army, for that matter, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, when the British Battalion was fully deployed in Central Bosnia and ready to operate, can you describe what the situation was like at the time between the ABiH and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: As we deployed, there was tension and some battles going on between the BiH and the HVO. As I brought my battalion group in across the mountains, 220 kilometres from the south, we were very worried that we would actually be blocked by the fighting around Novi Travnik and particularly there at that time, but previous to that when I was on the reconnaissance and in the setting-up stage, when I was on my own in Central Bosnia, there had been some quite serious incidents and fighting which sustained itself over perhaps a couple of weeks, perhaps three weeks, between the BiH and the HVO around the town of Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Vitez. So it wasn't a particularly -- it wasn't a particularly easy environment in which we had to set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, when you moved in, was the situation you found yourself in, was it as it was described to you before you deployed or was it different?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the British really, Your Honours, had no idea what was happening in Central Bosnia. The only briefing I had in the Ministry of Defence was one and a half hours on the history of the Balkans, which ended with the death of Tito ten years before. There was a briefing in Zagreb given by various people, including Colonel Mark Cook who was the commander of the medical unit, and a major, Major Colin Doyle, who had worked with Carrington or Owen. But that was it. It was general, and it was helpful insofar as it gave us a flavour, but the truth of the matter is I had no intelligence, real intelligence, what I would call intelligence on what was happening in Central Bosnia, Northern Bosnia, and Tomislavgrad down in the south until I found it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, did you expect when you arrived to see the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fighting each other?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but as I knew nothing about what was going on, I hoped I -- I wasn't too surprised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, initially who did you deal with, both with the HVO and the ABiH, and what can you tell us about those persons?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Firstly, Blaskic, Kordic for the HVO, and initially until I met Enver Hadzihasanovic, Dzemal Merdan for the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could you tell us about those persons in a few words; Blaskic, Kordic, Merdan, and Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Blaskic was a professional officer. I liked him, and I thought he would help. Kordic was not a professional officer. He was okay, but he was -- seemed to me a bit unguided or unwired. Merdan, Merdan is a fantastic officer. In my view from the start totally trustworthy. And Enver Hadzihasanovic was not far off that either. I knew Merdan more than Enver Hadzihasanovic, but I had great respect for both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Let us now move to January of 1993, and I would simply ask, what was the focus of your attention towards the middle Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: The real problem for January 1993 was fighting around Gornji Vakuf. The Commander Siljeg of the HVO was pushing north from Tomislavgrad with tanks and artillery, trying to take or destroy Gornji Vakuf. I had a company in Gornji Vakuf, and I spent at least two weeks plus every day on the ground in Gornji Vakuf trying to stop the fighting. And on the 13th of January, my driver was killed, my escort driver was shot as he drove his armoured Warrior through Gornji Vakuf. So January was not a good month for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, how did the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina react to the offensive being carried on by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I thought they were fighting rifles with sticks. The combatants, the distance between the opposing forces was well out of rifle range. The rifle, any rifle, has a combat range of 200 to 300 metres, Your Honours. Even a hand-held anti-tank missile, maximum range 500 metres. And the way this battle was taking place was with maximum safety to the HVO, who were using artillery, mortars, rocket launchers, and tanks, all of which had a range that could easily allow them to engage at something of the order of a thousand metres plus, apart from the mortars -- no, sorry, the mortars, the 81-millimetre mortars got 5.000 metres. So it was a very unequal contest and Siljeg was actually attacking Gornji Vakuf by the simple process of attrition, destroying house after house, and I really didn't know what to do about it. I just was actually was doing my very best to try to stop the fighting because my instructions from the United Nations were effectively to be convoy escorts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, at this stage how did the ABiH react, from your observations? Did they retaliate? Did they hold back? What -- how did they react?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I don't think they could have done anything because the battle range for which they had effective weapons was too short. But equally, when I had -- and I spoke to all the commanders on the ground and the representatives from 3rd Corps and the HVO representatives led by Siljeg, quite frankly the BiH just did not want this battle and it was probably caused, or we assumed from our intelligence, our assessment was that it was caused because perhaps Gornji Vakuf had been given to the Bosnian Croats in the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, can you help us just with the -- more information concerning the gentleman you name as being Siljeg. Who is he in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, he -- he was the -- he was the commander of the southern region of Bosnia for the HVO, and my assessment was that Siljeg - let's call him Brigadier Siljeg - commanded that region and based it on Tomislavgrad. And the central region of the HVO was commanded by Blaskic/Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'd like now to show you some documents which I will use throughout your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to ask the usher to give us the files, the binders with the documents, and we have a sufficient number of copies for all the parties in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, as these documents are being distributed, I would like to have the answer to one question, and that is did you have access in your capacity as commander of the British Battalion to orders or other correspondence being exchanged by the warring factions, either between themselves or internally, to any of them, and did you expect to have access to these documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't expect to have access to any such documents because my instructions were to remain neutral. Sometimes I had access to documents that I particularly initiated, perhaps a cease-fire agreement, and sometimes we might, within my organisation although I cannot recall, have been given command documents, but I cannot recall seeing any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if I would show you some of these documents, some of the orders issued by either the HVO or the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would you feel that you would be able to help us as to whether these documents reflect the situation that you lived in Central Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I will certainly do my best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Colonel, to turn to tab 3 of the binder that you have in front of you. I would ask you that -- to read this document and tell me if it reflects the situation as you saw it in January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: May I just look at my diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may the witness consult his diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's right. I think situation is reflected there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the record, the document in English is number 3. It is DH0561.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Colonel, I'd like to draw your attention to this document, and can you tell me whether what comes out of this document is that the HVO were attacking in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me, Colonel, what the purpose of this document would be from a command point of view, and I draw your attention to the last two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: This is an instruction by a commander to try and establish a cease-fire among his units. The development of outright hostilities in Gornji Vakuf over this period worried me a great deal, and I think I received a request, maybe from Commander Hadzihasanovic, to try and help. And I know that from now on, I was in the field practically for most of the day and most of the night, down in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask you now, Colonel, to turn to document at tab number 2. This document, for the needs of the transcript, is DH0557. Can you tell us, Colonel, what the commander is trying to do with this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: This is an instruction to not allow -- not allow the situation to escalate for soldiers of the BiH, to exercise great caution and not to do anything such as open fire unless it was absolutely necessary. I would interpret this document, as a commander receiving it, that I wasn't to open fire unless I actually had to do so to defend life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you think of any reasons why this action of General Hadzihasanovic was good or bad in the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the BiH in Gornji Vakuf were trying to just hold the line. It wasn't just that they were -- by Bugojno they had the Bosnian Serb army within a few kilometres. I mean, a -- again an impossible situation for any commander down there. And this is an instruction to say, "Look, let's not make it worse. Please, please, don't open fire. Don't give the HVO an excuse to attack us."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now turn, Colonel, to tab number 1. And this is a document which bears the number DH0554. And, Colonel, I would ask you to help us with what General Hadzihasanovic is trying to do with this document.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: It doesn't say it here, but I'm making the assumption that this is a request from Enver Hadzihasanovic to the BiH command to say, he's already in a conflict with the Bosnian Serb army, front lines at Bugojno, and this, I assume, is a request to ask them should he enter into conflict with the HVO, because actually there was enough -- there was enough fighting towards his units already, and he had to -- he would have the morale of his soldiers to think about. How do soldiers on the front line sit there and take, time after time, incoming fire and are ordered not to respond in any way? That is very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, could General Hadzihasanovic, could he not simply order to respond by himself without going to his superior headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sure he could have ordered to respond without going to superior headquarters, but Enver Hadzihasanovic, the one thing he isn't is unintelligent, and he would be trying hard to maintain the status quo with the HVO, because the situation is difficult enough there already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you see a reason why the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina would like to avoid a conflict at all costs with the HVO at this particular moment when you are in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, to me it's obvious: They're very stretched. They don't have ammunition. They don't have weapons. They don't have reinforcements. They don't want to fight with the HVO. This was apparent right the way through my tour. It was not -- most times that I ever got close to the fighting, which was quite a lot, actually, I never saw actually the HVO -- sorry, the BiH starting something. It was normally a reaction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina involved into any other battles at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: All over. The front line stretched intermittently from the area of Tomislavgrad throughout Bugojno. I mean, we had to make extensive diversions to get into Central Bosnia to avoid crossing the front lines. And then they went up to, you know, Travnik, then north of Travnik, up to Maglaj, and all the way up to Tuzla. I mean, it -- it was a massive front line to defend. And it wasn't like the First World War; it wasn't trench systems. Fundamentally, it was sort of centres of resistance, but to try and cross them is very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'll now ask you to turn to document number 4, which is also an order issued by General Hadzihasanovic. For the transcript, this document bears the number DH0562.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Colonel, what General Hadzihasanovic is trying to do with this order?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: If you look at the subparagraphs, "Firmly hold the lines reached toward the Chetniks," would be read as: Hold the line against the Bosnian Serb army in the region of Bugojno and elsewhere; stand by to repel HVO attacks, second line. Increase the state of alert of all units. Make sure that Dzemal Merdan who at the time was collocated with my company, B Company, is informed and coordinates and is actually the responsible coordinator commander in the region. And by the way, we also had HVO officers in my base at the same time. And this is important by all means to prevent the conflict from spreading. I think that's terribly important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, could you comment on the last paragraph. Why would a commander feel the need to put this comment at the end of his order?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Because the soldiers are going to be really angry. How would you like to have your butt kicked and not be able to respond? Effectively that's what's happening to these BiH soldiers. And I'm sorry to put it in those terms, Your Honour, but that's actually how soldiers view it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'll now ask you to turn to tab number 5, which is a document coming from BH command in Kiseljak and dated the 17th of January, 1993. As a first question, Colonel, can you tell us what is the BH command Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: This was the command headquarters of the United Nations under, at this time, General Phillippe Morillon, a French officer, now a member of the European Parliament and a friend. And BH command, then going up beyond that, UN headquarters had another headquarters in Zagreb. And this is -- I think this is going to Bosnia-Herzegovina command in Zagreb from Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the object of this document, Colonel, and who is it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: This is a demand by the HVO. It refers to a demand by the HVO which I remember very well because I was infuriated by it, that fundamentally the BiH unconditionally surrender in Gornji Vakuf, which, quite frankly, was totally against the expectation of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why would such a document be addressed, Colonel, to -- I look at the box in the top part where it says General Halilovic and Brigadier Petkovic. Do you know who these individuals are, and why would such a document be addressed to them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Because they are the representative chiefs of staff of the BiH and the HVO. So they are -- this is a warning document that this action by the HVO is well-noted and probably illegal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if I bring you to --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: May I just say that's probably who this document is directed to rather than the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I draw your attention to the last line, last sentence in paragraph 1, where it says: "We further believe that both the Bosnian Presidency forces and the HVO are moving reinforcements into the area in preparation for hostilities." Can you comment on this specific sentence in terms of its impact on the situation in Gornji Vakuf, or its potential impact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: If you have a fire and you put petrol on it, it becomes a bigger fire. This is a reinforcement which is understandable from a military perspective, but it becomes political dynamite and will make a serious, serious war start quickly. And that is the reason why I wanted to stay in Gornji Vakuf as long as possible, to try and get some kind of truce, some kind of ceasefire organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, what -- could the ABiH and the HVO bring in reinforcements, if you know, based on what you saw on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: The HVO would reinforce from the south with no problem. They would come across the mountains from Tomislavgrad. The BiH would have much more of a problem because there was, as I understand it, as I recall, HVO units blocking the routes -- route south. But equally, they did try. I recall they did try to reinforce as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I now ask you to turn to tab number 7. Now, this is a document which is addressed from the head of the Regional Centre Split and addressed to Zagreb. Do you know, what is the Regional Centre in Split and to which headquarters this document is addressed to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: This is not something I saw, but it looks to me like the European Community Monitoring Mission documents, and it looks to me like the ambassador sending a report to his headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you quickly glance through this document and say what the ambassador is reporting to his headquarters in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, he -- this gentleman, Mr. Beaussou, another very good French diplomat, had chaired a meeting at probably my request between the HVO and the BiH in Gornji Vakuf. The local commander of the HVO -- actually, it was very difficult to get Siljeg. I sometimes had to go and get him myself to these meetings. Siljeg says that two of his soldiers had been killed by snipers, which was possible, I don't know, and he used that as an excuse to break it up. And it was just an example, yet just another example of many that I witnessed of delaying tactics with regard to trying to get some kind of peace, peaceful situation. I mean, the two men may have been killed, but as I remember, so many civilians were dying at the time it astonished me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like to draw your attention the second paragraph, where you see the number 2 being there, and then there is a paragraph right below this, and the paragraph reads as follows: "What is at stake there is not a local problem. The two local commanders did not look very much like enemies. It's certainly a political purpose close to ethnic cleansing." Would you agree with this conclusion and were you able to notice such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I thought was happening and that this was some kind of preemptive move. Which I could never understand. Why would they preemptively take a place if they were going to be handed it anyway? Why would they destroy it? But quite frankly, my read intelligence-wise, the purpose of attacking Gornji Vakuf was to take it in anticipation of the plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I ask you now to turn to tab number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just before we do that, if the record could be reflected that we discussed in tab 7 DH0648.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my colleague for this remark. I forgot to mention it. Perhaps my colleague will be using the document later on during his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I now turn to this document at tab number 8, and this is a document dated on the 25th of January, 1993. I would like you to take a few minutes to look at this document while I request permission from the Chamber to use the document because it is, in fact, a new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a document on which will figure on our final list of documents. This document has been disclosed to the Prosecution, and we ask for permission to be able to use it with today's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to direct your attention to this document and to go to the third page and let us know, if you can, what this document is talking about and whether you were involved in any way with this document or with the events discuss in this document.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I was trying to get the fighting to stop, and if you look at the third page, it refers to the conditions laid down by Siljeg, the HVO commander, which was unconditional surrender. It refers to the fact that I told Colonel Siljeg that he would answer for all his crimes one day - some hope - and I pointed out that the deliberate targeting of civilians was a crime against humanity. I'm sorry, Your Honours, I'm probably incorrect in my legal understanding what a crime against humanity is, but whatever it is, shooting, shelling civilians is against the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, the information contained as to what was happening, who was it addressed to, how and why? I'm talking about the third page, where it says at paragraph 2, "The commander of 1 Cheshire has spent the last five days in Gornji Vakuf."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I was the commander of the 1st Cheshires, and I -- I got through to the commander of British forces in Split by my national means, because I was so frustrated by the lack of UN action to actually achieve anything. We'd been there for so long, and meanwhile the town was being shelled to bits. I'd lost soldiers and had wounded, and I got through to the commander of the British forces and I pleaded with him -- well, didn't plead, I just said, Can you do it? He said yes, and he contacted Geneva and spoke to Lord Owen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the second page of this document, specifically at paragraph number 2, do you believe that this is linked to what you did, and were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, I wasn't aware of what was happening as a consequence of my request to Brigadier Cummings, the British commander, because I was overwhelmed by the situation, but it might be that I had some influence in getting something done at the top to try and stop this fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the order at the end of this document issued by Petkovic as a cease-fire, did you use this document and how did this cease-fire actually take place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I was in a conference room, a conference room at Gornji Vakuf. It wasn't a conference room, it was a room with chairs and a table. And I was chairing the meeting. Siljeg was there, and so I think was Merdan and various other people. And I was summoned away from the table and told that Petkovic had given instructions that the fighting by the HVO was to stop immediately. And I didn't have any paper on it, I was just told that had come from Geneva. I went back into the conference room and I said to Siljeg I had received information that the fighting was to stop immediately and he was to do that on my word, but it seemed to me from the look on his face that he knew that already before he had come to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Do you remember after getting this cease-fire, after two weeks of intensive work in Gornji Vakuf, do you recall what you did next in your actions as commander of BritBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall getting back to your battalion? Did you go back to your battalion or did you get involved in any specific activities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: If I might, I would find out by looking at my diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would refer you to your diary, then, for the date of 25 January 1993. Now, my first question, Colonel, before you look at this page of your diary, is: While you were in Gornji Vakuf, were you aware of what was going on in Busovaca during the same time frame?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I was aware of it, but I couldn't deal with it personally because I felt my point of concentrated effort had to be down in Gornji Vakuf. So it would be dealt with by my second in command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, I ask you to look at the document at tab number 9, which is a milinfosum dated 21 January, 1993, which is the period you were in Gornji Vakuf, and I ask you to look at section 2 on page 2 where it says "Busovaca," and whether you can tell me know whether this paragraph reflects information that you were aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the LiveNote, this document bears the number DH612, and at this stage it has been marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware. This is the Kacuni checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us, Colonel, about the Kacuni checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it was on the main supply route into Sarajevo via Kiseljak. It was a place quite close to the front line positions of BiH and HVO, and it was established by the ABiH, and it was quite difficult for us to break through it. Not break through it, negotiate our way through it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we'll get back into future questions on the checkpoint itself, but I draw your attention to the middle of the document, where it says that: "Between 2000 Alpha and 2100 Alpha..." so 8.00 and 9.00 in the evening "... two HVO checkpoints were erected at either end of the town centre. ... At approximately the same time a quad of 50 cal. mounted on a flatbed was deployed on the road south of the town ... All main roads in and out of Busovaca were then controlled." And between 9.00, or 2100, Alpha and 0200 Alpha, or 2.00 in the morning, "... the Dutch transport squadron reported a number of explosions in the town. And on the 21st of January a daylight recce confirmed that eight shops had been badly damaged by fire and some form of explosive." Now, at the end of the document, it says, "The attack of 20/21 January 1993 appears to be a pre-planned, coordinated attack on the Muslim population." Were you aware of this situation while you were in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, in general, but not in detail, because I had to hand over responsibility for that area, probably to my second in command or my Operations Officer. But, yes, I am still responsible for what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, as you travelled back from Gornji Vakuf into the area of Busovaca and Kacuni, what was the situation like when you returned? And now, of course, you can, as you requested, look at your diary for the date of 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we had the main route into Sarajevo, the main supply route, the most important route to actually resupply by land, Sarajevo, blocked by at least three new roadblocks, which was totally counter to the way I wanted things to happen because I was very conscious that not just my -- I was not just responsible for my area, I was responsible for ensuring that convoys got into Sarajevo to help the people of Sarajevo. And this did not help. So that was a driver for me, to try and open these roadblocks. And yes, Busovaca was cut off, probably commanded, I think at the time by Kordic, and I think at some stage I visited Kordic, and I certainly went down to Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, based on your diary, and I draw your attention to the second last paragraph from the bottom on the 25th. Do you recall what actions if any were taken concerning the checkpoint or the roadblock set up by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina army and what you felt about this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I was quite angry about this checkpoint. It was a big lorry, Your Honour, cross -- across the road, with logs on it, and they had put the tires down. It was difficult to move a lorry like that quickly. And I went -- I sent one of my company commanders, Major Philip Jennings, and told him don't come back unless you've got this thing opened. And he hadn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel did you -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: He hadn't. I went down, and I think I went with -- I went to 3 Corps headquarters, asked Merdan to accompany me, and went down there with him, I think, but my diary might not be specific on that. I know that I somehow got it opened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, in your diary it says in the second to last paragraph that from your battalion headquarters you received information that the corps commander had agreed that the two Warriors could replace the checkpoint. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, I do. Sorry. I do. We put two Warriors there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your diary then says that you went to the commander of the 3rd Corps that evening to complain that they had really started this trouble. Do you recall this visit to General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It's typical of both of us that we would go and complain. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. certainly would go and complain, because that really infuriated me, that roadblock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end of this page on the 25 of September [sic], it basically says that you arranged a cease-fire for 6.00 on the 26th of January with General Hadzihasanovic while Brigadier Roddy Cordy-Simpson was doing the same with Blaskic in Kiseljak. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. This was a coordinated effort on both our parts. Roddy Cordy-Simpson, I knew that Blaskic was in his headquarters in Kiseljak so I requested that he would go and do that and I would go and see Enver Hadzihasanovic. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask you, Colonel, to turn to tab number 10 in your binder and let me know whether this document, issued on the 25th of January by General Hadzihasanovic, is actually the cease-fire that you had arranged with him that evening.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is, because the date is exact: 0600, 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there's an error in the transcript, probably made by me. Page 33, line 3. There's mention of the 25th of September, but it should be the 25th of January. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Colonel, so this would be the order issued by General Hadzihasanovic in response to your request for a cease-fire at 6.00 on the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll now ask you to turn to tab 11, and actually to take a quick look at tabs 11, 12, and 13, and inform us what General Hadzihasanovic is trying to do with those three correspondence addressed to the commander of the Central Operative Zone of the HVO in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just for the sake of the record, if my learned colleague could always indicate if he refers to tabs which actual exhibit numbers he means that have already been introduced because later it's almost impossible to trace back the exhibits if we talk about tabs as opposed to DH and then the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It would be better to say document 632, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. After these three documents, Mr. President, we will have a break. I have one more question about these documents. I would like us to leave the binder with the witness so that we can speed things up after the break, if my colleague has no objection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Colonel, as the last question before the break, can you tell us what General Hadzihasanovic is trying to do with those documents? And I will, for the sake of the transcript, say the document at tab 11 is number 0632; the document at tab 12 is 0633; and the document at tab 13 is 0634. Colonel, what in your opinion is General Hadzihasanovic trying to do with those three documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: He's trying to say to the HVO commander that some -- some rumours or propaganda put out is not true, that people have not been so-called ethnically cleansed from various areas. He's trying to say that there should be -- he should cease fire immediately. He's also trying to stop multiple rocket launchers and Nora, which we always called a 155-millimetre gun, firing. So he's requesting or ordering, if he can order the HVO, but certainly Commander Hadzihasanovic certainly knew Blaskic. They were old acquaintances at the very least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how is he proposing to solve the situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Now you have me for the moment. I haven't read -- is there a solution to this? I can't see. Stop firing is the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe we can look -- Colonel, I will leave you those documents for you to look at at the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think we can have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to have the break, Colonel. During the break, you may consult the binder so that you will be able to respond more quickly to the questions that will continue to be put to you. We will resume at about ten past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please have a word with somebody to lower the temperature in the courtroom. It seems to be very hot, maybe 30 something degrees. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Welcome back, Colonel. When we left before the break you informed the Trial Chamber that yourself had arranged a cease-fire for the 26th of January at 6.00, with General Hadzihasanovic, while Cordy-Simpson, Roddy Cordy-Simpson did the same with Blaskic in a concerted effort. You confirmed that the order issued by General Hadzihasanovic with respect to the issuing of the cease-fire, and we were just discussing those three documents at tabs 11, 12, and 13 concerning measures that were taken by General Hadzihasanovic with his counterpart in the HVO. And again for the transcript, these are documents DH632 for identification, documents DH633 for identification, and document DH634 for identification. Now, having looked at those documents, Colonel, can you tell me, looking at tab 13, the first paragraph, what General Hadzihasanovic is proposing to do to resolve the situation in this area.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: He is proposing that there be delegations between both sides, should meet and somehow sort out any problems that there are. And of course I would either provide an officer or be part of it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you say, Colonel, that this was the good course of action for General Hadzihasanovic in the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I refer to your diary for 26th of January, there is a paragraph in the morning that deals with your reaction when Philip Jennings who was, I guess, officer commanding of one of your companies, had problems with the roadblock in Kacuni and that you contacted Dzemal Merdan in Zenica. Do you recall this incident and can you provide us information in this respect?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I was upset because this roadblock was still not open, Your Honour, and I dispatched an officer to sort it out; Major Jennings. He failed, and so I was quite angry. And so I telephoned Mr. Merdan in Zenica and I said the Muslims -- the Bosnian BiH were in some way to blame because the roadblock was still not open, and they said -- I said they were holding me up. And Mr. Merdan offered to come and help me open it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Merdan show up, and how was the situation resolved, if it was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, he did come and we went together to the roadblock, and then at this point I witnessed a problem from the BiH because they wouldn't accept Mr. Merdan's instructions to open the roadblock. And then after awhile of discussion, it was agreed and I pressed and I spoke to the command as well, and I assured him that I would be leaving two Warriors there to ensure the safety of the roadblock, is the way I put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this apparent lack of control that you are describing, was this an isolated incident or is this something that saw on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I saw it on several occasions because local BiH were not necessarily totally understanding how command and control should work. And indeed, there were often quite heated exchanges when people like Mr. Merdan tried to give instructions to say open the roadblock or stop this, stop that. There were quite heated exchanges, which I think stemmed -- came from the fact that these HVO people were local people defending their own homes, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, would you -- in the end was the incident resolved? Was the roadblock actually removed or at least replaced by those two Warriors that you are mentioning?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was indeed. But it took a while. So my anger with Major Jennings was unfounded and I sometimes feel sorry that I was angry with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask you, Colonel, to go to tab 14, which is a milinfosum number 87, dated the 26th of January. I would ask you to look at page 2 at the top, the section called Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a new document that has been added to the list. This is a milinfosum and the date is 26 January. I would like to ask the Chamber to allow me to discuss this document with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this, Colonel, the paragraph that describes what happened at the Kacuni checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now refer to you tab 15. This document bears the number 1738, and I would ask you to say what General Hadzihasanovic is doing with this document and what is he ordering to the commander of the 333 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: This is a clear instruction to 333rd Brigade that they are to remove the barricade, stop any kind of bad behaviour such as looting, and have a decent attitude towards the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you ever made aware that this order was actually issued in this form?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Not in a written form, but I certainly believed that Commander or General Hadzihasanovic - I will now call him General Hadzihasanovic - was actually doing his very best to get the situation under control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in general throughout your tour in Bosnia, when General Hadzihasanovic committed to something to you, did you have any reason to believe that he would not honour his word?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: The only time he would not be able to honour his word is if people wouldn't actually obey him. But in those circumstances, he would make strenuous efforts to try and make sure that his word was kept by perhaps dispatching Dzemal Merdan down to the local area, or some other staff officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, also in your diary for the 26th of January, towards the middle of the page, there is a reference to a meeting to negotiate a cease-fire, which is chaired by Roddy Cordy-Simpson and attended by Mr. Merdan and Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask that you turn to tab 16, which is Exhibit P133, and by looking at this document, whether it accurately reflects what happened during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: It ties up with my diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you believe what Blaskic said about people having been killed for which he stopped the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have been very generous in not objecting a couple of times, leading or asking the Colonel to comment on documents which, you know, it has not been established that he saw it and so on, but here just for the sake of clarity, before he answers, that it be established whether he was at this meeting, because according to the document it didn't say so. So before these general comments are made about whether Blaskic says something or whether you believe that it was true, that the proper foundation be established. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Colonel, did you attend this meeting which I -- which you acknowledge as being recorded in your diary for the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend it. I went down in a Warrior to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened at the meeting and whether it was successful in reaching a cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I think it was not successful in reaching a cease-fire agreement for the reason that Blaskic said seven people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when Blaskic said that seven people had been killed being the reason to stop the meeting, did you believe him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know, to be honest. I don't -- you know, how did I know whether seven people had been killed or, indeed, how many people had been killed. But that was the reason used for the meeting to be stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what was Roddy Cordy-Simpson's attitude towards stopping the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, he wanted it to continue and get a cease-fire regardless of this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the conclusion at the end of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I think that we were to meet again tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document at tab 16, document P133, does it reflect what happened at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it does, because General Cordy-Simpson was persistent in trying to get the negotiations regardless of the reports of seven people killed, and he insisted on another meeting the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, in your diary it is reported that that day getting back was a performance and that it was difficult for you to accompany Dzemal Merdan back to Zenica. My question to you is: During this trip to Zenica, did you speak to Dzemal Merdan about the allegations made by Blaskic at the meeting and, if so, did Dzemal Merdan mention anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: It's not in my diary, Your Honour. It's highly likely I would have mentioned it, but I can't with truth say I did, and that is the best of my recollection. I would normally mention it, but I can't -- I haven't got a record that I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall anything that Dzemal Merdan would have said at that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, his normal reaction was to promise to investigate it, and I believed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving down to your -- again on the 27th of January in your diary, there is a mention of a second meeting taking place on the 27th of January. Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: We reached a cease-fire agreement and Blaskic seemed to have changed his mind on the sticking point, which was the seven people being killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what, if anything, Merdan said at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: No, I don't. I mean, I have to say it's very difficult for me to remember the detail, Your Honour, at this time. Even getting there we were attacked several times each day. God knows by who.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I'd like to refer you to tab 17, which is document DH0664. My first question, and this is something I may have missed at the beginning, can you tell the Trial Chamber who Roddy Cordy-Simpson is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: At the time Brigadier Roddy Cordy-Simpson was the chief of staff to General Morillon, General Morillon being the French UN commander for Bosnia, and General Roddy Cordy-Simpson being a British officer attached under command of General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, this is the minutes of the meeting of the 27th of January. Did you attend this meeting? Is this the meeting that is referred to at the bottom of the page dealing with 27 January in your diary?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you take a look at this document and see whether it refreshes your memory as to what may have been said by the parties during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I think that at this meeting, Dzemal Merdan made a report that he thought seven HVO soldiers had been killed and that it wasn't on a cease-fire negotiation as such -- it wasn't a hand-over of prisoners, rather, it was actually fighting, a skirmish, and he made that report and accepted that actually seven were killed. I think that is what has happened, and I seem to recall it although I can't read this stuff at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if I refer your attention to the next page of this document, and more specifically to paragraphs 8 and 9, paragraph 8 says that all parties signed the agreement, which is to be found at Annex A, and after the signing of the agreement, the three parties involved informed the press about the achievements. Do you recall this being the result of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at paragraph 9, it says that, "During the break, the negotiations were put at risk by the HVO allegation of the burning and shelling of Busovaca from Fojnica. Quick verification of the rumours with the UN forces in those villages proved that they were totally unfounded. The HVO agreed on continuing the negotiations." Do you recall if this happened and how it happened during the break at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it was my operational area, Your Honour, and I got on the radio and spoke to my operations room, and I said I want a report as to anyone in that area, has this happened? The answer came back no, it hasn't. So I reported back immediately to the meeting that, in my view, nothing had happened, and then it continued again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this allegation by the HVO, was it the same as the seven people in Dusina or a different one?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: No. This is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your diary at the bottom of page -- of the day for the 27th of September --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: January, sorry. That's the second time I do this, if not more. That there was a performance over an alleged atrocity committed by the Bosnian Muslims, or the ABiH. Do you recall what this in your diary refers to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: When I use the word "performance," I mean a story, a something to make a problem, something like that. To be quite honest, I don't know whether this "performance" refers to the killing of seven HVO soldiers or the performance of burning and attacking Busovaca, but it will be one of those two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the paragraph 11 on the next page of this document, it talks about the setting up of the joint commission.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whose idea it was to set up the joint commission and how it took place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
