utterances.text: You know, I don't know whose idea it was. It might have been mine, but it was a good idea, but it might have been someone else too. The commission was essentially to travel around to try and get to the bottom of what had happened at various incidents, to try and take away the irritations that would cause the HVO and the BiH to come into conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, in this paragraph 11, it says that the commission is to be set up as of the 28th of January, that they are to travel around to where there were allegations of problems, and that they are to report at the meeting on 30 January. Do you recall this being what was said about the joint commission on that day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I recall everything except the date in my brain, but the date I can't confirm that we agreed the 30th of January. But that was exactly the way we wanted it. We wanted it set up fast, we wanted to operate with sufficient authority from the top, and we wanted -- to be quite honest, I didn't really want to be involved in it because I just didn't have any more officers left, so I really wanted the ECM, the European Community Monitoring Mission to do this task, and to that end I gave them some vehicles, but I just did not want any more of my officers used on this sort of task. We were stretched enough as it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that they were supposed to report to you on the 30th of January after having visited the locations where there were alleged violations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, absolute -- well, you say the 30th of January. I now see it's the 30th of January, so I confirm that's the case, but I don't remember the 30th of January. Everything else is accurate in my mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mention the report made by Mr. Merdan with respect to those seven people having been killed, and you said earlier that he mentioned that people had been killed but during fighting and not during a prisoner exchange. Did you believe what Mr. Merdan said at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I did. I did, because the HVO had alleged it and Mr. Merdan had confirmed it. So why should I not believe that if both sides are in agreement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There seemed to be a difference with the fact that the HVO is saying that a crime was committed and Mr. Merdan is saying that no crime was committed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: My position was that I was most crucially concerned about civilians dying. These were soldiers, and apparently there was a firefight between two sides who customarily shot at one another, and that was well known. So I had no more time for this matter. It had been investigated to the best of the ability of both sides, and I actually had had more pressing matters to deal with than actually going further into this matter. But the European Community Monitoring Mission, this commission would go there. After all, Mr. Merdan was part of it and if General Hadzihasanovic was prepared to allow his deputy to be used at a time when all sides were stretched and totally without sleep, I thought that was putting it pretty high, frankly. So I was satisfied by this. And Blaskic appointed his second in command, too, at a time when they could have been getting so little sleep it's almost impossible to think they were awake during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the meeting about the 30th of January, do you recall this meeting? You may not recall, of course, the date 30 January, but this is the meeting you actually chaired. Do you recall this meeting, looking at your notes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how this meeting was conducted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I chaired it, Your Honour, and I asked Mr. Jeremy Fleming of the European Community Monitoring Mission, who was leading the commission, to make a report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the report that you -- that he had been asked to prepare at the meeting of the 27th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask you to turn to tab 18, which is document P922. You probably saw this document at the break. I would ask you to look at the report made by Mr. Fleming on page 2. And more specifically, the fact that they had -- the third paragraph from the bottom, where it says: "We visited the town of Busovaca."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Mr. Fleming and his commission visit Dusina and report on what they had seen in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I think Dusina was visited by one of my patrols, possibly with Mr. Fleming. I think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when this report was given, did you have any doubts as to the fact that those seven people had actually been killed by a crime and not during fighting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I think it was criminal for anyone to fight in Central Bosnia, to be honest. So it was certainly a crime that these people had been killed. Whether it was a crime that we could do anything about was another matter. As the bodies apparently were picked, and I think by Sergeant Kujawinski of my battle group, I think there was no doubt that seven were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But these are -- who is -- Sergeant Kujawinski?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who he is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: He was one of the -- he was one of the platoon sergeants of my battle group, and I think he went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I refer you to your diary, Colonel, for the 30th of January. And if you can just read quickly the part about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is this the incident in which Sergeant Kujawinski was involved or is this the incident in Dusina that we were talking a little earlier about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I'm confused. Forgive me. I'm not sure. I think Sergeant Kujawinski might have been involved in Miletici early -- later on. So forgive me, Your Honour. There are so many incidents, and I'm only an infantry officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this incident in Dusina, those seven people, Colonel, just to -- can you confirm what your belief was at the end of that meeting on the 30th with respect to whether you were satisfied it had been investigated and with the result of that investigation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: As I couldn't understand why seven people would be killed, I thought it was probably the work of Mujahedin. There would be no reason whatsoever for this sort of -- I just did -- I didn't have time to investigate it, but I probably thought the BiH -- seven people killed? You know, that's -- that's almost a deliberate attack. You know, one or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. two people killed in a firefight, yes. Seven people, that looks to start like being a massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I may bring you back, Colonel, just to the account of Mr. Merdan, because you mentioned that you were satisfied with Mr. Merdan's account. So I just want to make sure that we're not confusing different incidents.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that I could be confusing different incidents. There are so many incidents. Forgive me, Your Honour. I think you might find that Mr. Merdan's account was accepted by me, and I might be referring to another incident that followed a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The only point: What's sometimes troubling, first of all, when he refers to his diary, if he could perhaps read out these parts - I know my learned colleague wants to save time - so it's reflected, you know, at what time he refreshed his memory, because we do have the diary, and I have absolutely no objections if it's introduced into -- as evidence. And I also believe he already testified at what Merdan told him and whether he appreciated what he told him and it's now rehashing. So I don't think that's helpful, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Colonel, let's go on to this meeting of the 30th having been done and this agreement reached. Do you recall another meeting which took place on the 1st of February?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: With General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And if you can look at your diary and maybe read the paragraph that you have in your diary about this meeting, if you do not remember, or if you could just tell us what the meeting was about.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I -- I have the greatest of respect for General Morillon, and I was being quite rude about the general in the paragraph I wrote, and I -- I can repeat it, but I don't see any point in doing so. This was a short meeting to establish a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this meeting on the 1st of February, and who attended the meeting, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Blaskic, Hadzihasanovic, General Morillon, and myself. And also my successor was present, Alistair Duncan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I refer you now to a -- if you can look at tab 21, which is Exhibit P137, and see whether this document allows you to know who the people were at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. This is the same meeting. Forgive me. My diary didn't have the full list. It fundamentally is a confirmation meeting to try and ensure the cease-fire between the HVO and the ABiH continued and that we had access to all -- down all routes and that the commission continued its work to try and stop problems when they arose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, you mentioned that normally Mr. Merdan's react when you made any allegations to him, can you recall what was Mr. Merdan's normal reaction?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, sometimes he knew of the allegation already, but his normal reaction was to do all he could to investigate it. He promised that, and I believed him. And I would also say, you know, to bring -- investigate and to bring people who have done wrong to justice, if possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that ever an undertaking that was given to you by General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I can't recall a date, but certainly that was my belief in my meetings with General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask you, Colonel, to turn to tab 24, which is Exhibit P138. You may have looked at this order during the break. Can you quickly glance through it and explain what this order is issued by General Hadzihasanovic to all brigades on the 3rd of February.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: This is a reminder overall of the responsibilities of commanders to abide by the rules of law. This is a direct order from the commander to all units in the 3rd Corps that matters such as looting, burnings, imprisoning of civilians was unacceptable and was not to happen and that commanders who did such a thing would be held responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that a normal course of action or what you would expect from the parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: To be honest, it was a necessary course of action in the case of General Hadzihasanovic whose -- many of his officers probably had only heard of Geneva in terms of it being a city in Switzerland, because they were not military commanders. I think it's a good thing that he sent this order out, and I applaud that it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I refer you to the third paragraph of this order, which reads as follows: "Instruct legal organs in units to register such events and deal with them urgently in accordance with the regulations and the law." Is that a proper course of action for General Hadzihasanovic to take?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, and shows the quality of the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I refer you to paragraph 6 of this document, basically saying to "hold the commanders of brigades, independent units and municipal defence staff responsible for carrying out this order." What does it mean by "to hold commanders responsible"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, if the rule of law, the rules of war had been disobeyed, that the commanders of units that took part in such actions would be held responsible. It is the absolute duty of a commander to take responsibility for the actions of those subordinates underneath him. It doesn't mean he's at fault necessarily or to blame for them, but he should take responsibility in some of the blame.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at this order, Colonel, would you say that you are surprised by this order or that it just corresponds with your belief of what was happening within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it corresponds with my belief with what was happening within the 3rd Corps, and I'm not surprised but delighted to see it in writing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if I would show you a document which states that more than 1.000 soldiers from the 3rd Corps have been the object of criminal reports filed by the 3rd Corps and its subordinate units, how would you react to this hypothesis?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Then I would be surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In all -- in all fairness, that's impossible for him to answer. He needs to know for what crimes these people were persecuted. I think that's a general question which is impossible, unfair to answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can make my question more precise and I would most likely show you a document later on, but simply this document over 1.000 soldiers being the object of criminal reports for all kinds of criminal offences from stealing to looting to burning to murder and to offences against a person. You just mentioned that you would be surprised. Why would that be?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Because there was so much going on. I was surprised at the number of soldiers. That would probably be one-quarter of the corps, whatever the corps strength was, maybe 4.000, 5.000. That's a lot. But it does show that there was some kind of control over the soldiers and some kind of responsibility being expected by commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does that tell you about General Hadzihasanovic's attitude towards making reports?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, General Hadzihasanovic is actually someone who is quite precise, and he is a -- he was a commander under real pressure, and I think that he -- if he could, he would put it in writing so that people were under no illusion as to what was expected of them, if he could. Mindful of the fact that he probably didn't have much time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I'd like to move on to the events of April 1993. And those events are discussed into your diary, and more specifically I'd like to refer where you speak on the 15th of April about the kidnapping of the HVO Brigade Commander Totic. Do you recall this incident, and what can you tell the Trial Chamber about this incident?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I was in Travnik in the middle of the afternoon, on foot, walking down to the town, and I received a radio message that a brigade commander of the HVO had been taken -- had been captured, had been taken as a hostage or something in Zenica. So I went straight back to my headquarters that was some five, six miles to the east, at Vitez, and then I received a message from Ambassador Thebault of the European Community Monitoring Mission saying, "I need you to come to Zenica immediately to join a meeting I'm having because we need your presence."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what -- who attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, certainly Ambassador Thebault was there. Dzemal Merdan was there, the chief of police was there. I think the mayor was there, mayor of Zenica. But I arrived late and the meeting was already taking -- already started. And I think it was in the Internacional Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything special that happened during this meeting or any specific contributions that you made during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I demanded that Dzemal Merdan sort this matter out immediately, that the BiH, who I made probably the incorrect assumption, had some kind of control over this situation, get Totic back. There were already, I think, two or three men dead as a result of this kidnapping, and I remember saying to Merdan that it wasn't good enough for the police -- for it to be a police investigation. We all had to get this sorted out quickly because I was fully aware from my intelligence that the whole of Central Bosnia was just about to blow like a volcano, with people in position to do great damage to civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Dzemal Merdan's response to you when you asked him to take the situation under control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: He said it was -- I think he said it was extremely difficult, and he implied that they had no contact with these people, something like that. And I said, well, he had to have contact with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he respond?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall what happened the next day, on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Of course I remember what happened on the 16th of April. The 16th April was a disaster. On that day, huge numbers of people were killed in the Lasva Valley by an attack centred around the village of Ahmici but also extending down the valley to Busovaca and into Vitez. It was a disaster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what you personally did on that day? And if you want to take a look at your diary, do so in terms of what actions you took that day.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I don't need the diary. I was in the wrong end. I was in the wrong position. I was in Zenica when I was woken up at 0500 by a message from my second in command saying that the whole of Central Bosnia was -- actually seemed to have been blowing up, and I immediately said I'd come back, but I was in the wrong -- I was trapped on the other side of the lines. Anyway, he suggested I wait until it was daylight, and the BiH roadblocks in Zenica were most unwilling to let me cross the mountain road, which is the back road. I insisted on it. And they, with reluctance, opened the barricade. I went through one, two, three roadblocks. Two of them were with mines, and I moved the mines. Anyway, suffice to say after about three-quarters of an hour on the road, I rejoined my battalion through an HVO roadblock at the bottom of the mountain road and the Lasva Valley. I then went straight into town to try -- I got in my Land Rover, and I went straight into town, to Vitez, to try and find Blaskic. And then I drove back into Zenica to try and find out what had happened with regard to the Totic matter. And I spent most of the day shuttling around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your aim in going to Vitez and in that area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I wanted to just try and speak with the commander of the HVO to try and stop what was clearly happening. I had seen a lot of bodies on the mountain as I'd come over the top. I was on my own. And I wanted to try and stop -- try and stop the fighting from the point of view of the HVO. The catalyst for this fighting could well have been the taking of Totic, and that was something I warned Merdan the day before and of course he knew that. And this is what happened. Now, whether in fact the taking of Totic was the catalyst for action or the spur for action or the reason, I'm not sure. All I know is that the forces were in position for offensive action by the HVO by the evening of the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you commented in many trials about Ahmici, and my purpose was not to come back on this incident, but you did say in previous trials that this was a well-planned and coordinated attack.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go to the 16th of April when you returned to Zenica. Did you attend any meetings that you recall, returning to Zenica on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I attended with Ambassador Thebault a meeting to try and find out where Totic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall if Dzemal Merdan was attending that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: The answer is I don't recall in my brain, I can't see it in my diary, but undoubtedly he would have been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall having a conversation with him concerning the -- the alleged people who would have done this kidnapping of Totic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I mean, it would be entirely the thrust of any conversation I had with Ambassador Thebault, with the mayor of Zenica, with the chief of police, and with Merdan. I'm quite sure I did, I was absolutely demanding that we must actually get Totic back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Merdan's response with respect to the people who allegedly did the kidnapping of Totic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: He didn't give me a satisfactory response because he just looked like he couldn't get an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I was angry, actually. I was angry because people were dying all over the place, and I just thought this was quite absurd, that why -- and the question was in my brain: Why would anyone do this in the position they're in? And of course I wasn't connecting too well at the time, but of course I understand it could well have been these Mujahedin people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just one -- before we go back to this idea of Mujahedin, did you succeed in getting a cease-fire on the 16th of April? Did you ever have a meeting to achieve a cease-fire on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I definitely positioned my armour to try and keep the two sides apart. For example, I put them on the main road overnight, which was very dangerous, actually, because they were being attacked by both sides. But on the road down the Lasva Valley, I can't remember -- my diary doesn't say. We did have a meeting in Zenica. Then I took -- the next day I think I took the European Community Monitoring Mission and the ICRC to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I refer you to the 16th of April when you are back in Vitez, was there a meeting to negotiate a cease-fire in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Highly likely and done by someone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: By my second in command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you take a look, Colonel, at tab 26. Can you tell us what this document is issued by commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone on the cessation of combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: This is a cease-fire document which there was an UNPROFOR representative, probably my second in command, but I could be inaccurate here. The 16th was a day of extreme busyness for me. I don't think I attended -- and you've got here -- you have also got Cerkez here at the meeting, and that would mean it would be in Vitez, and I spent most of my time on the road in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you look at page 3 of this document and tell us what you see in this document.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: God, this is a rescinding order. So at 1600 hours, the first document, you have Blaskic ordering an immediate cease-fire, but at 1500, an hour before -- there's something going wrong here. At 1500 hours, an hour before, Blaskic says, "Don't carry out that cease-fire."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is he instructing his troops to do about the order and about future instructions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: He is to keep -- he is to keep the first one handy, keep it handy. That's an English term. I don't know. It's strange. Keep it handy and use the first one if the United Nations Protection Force come near you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you react to such a document being issued by the commander of the central Operative Zone of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: That's a lie. That's a deceit. That's -- so in other words what effectively -- but there's a problem here because there's a 1500 time on one and 1600 on the other. They should be the reverse way round.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like to move on now to the 24th of April, 1993. If you can look in your diary for this date and tell us whether you had any meetings that day or what you were doing on the 24th of April.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I started by going into see Santic and Pero Skopljak, who were HVO officers in the PTT building of Vitez. I informed them that I considered it to be an utter and complete disgrace that Ahmici had occurred, that it was a total slur on the Bosnian Croats, that it was a disaster for Bosnian Croat politics, it should be investigated as soon as possible, it should be fully investigated with Bosnian Muslim representatives on the commission. Then I went to see Blaskic in Hotel Vitez. I pointed out that it was in his Operational Zone of responsibility, which he agreed, and told him he had to do something extremely positively about this, and I told him that I had already contacted the Security Council of the United Nations direct and asked them to come and visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if on the 24th of April the Security Council was actually in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were in Central Bosnia. I know that I sent a message to the permanent representatives for the Security Council who I believed were to visit Sarajevo and asked them to come and visit my headquarters as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that and how did this take place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but it was in the next few days, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall visiting any specific sites with the members of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I did. I briefed them in my headquarters. There were -- the president of the Security Council was the Venezuelan ambassador. I briefed the Security Council permanent representatives in my headquarters and I arranged transport to take them to see Ahmici, the massacre in Ahmici. I warned them there were other massacres in Central Bosnia alone, that this was not the only one, and I said that it was disgusting and I asked them if there was anything we could do to set up an International Criminal Court to try war criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, apparently I have exceeded the two hours planned. I would like to ask permission from the Chamber to continue until I finish very shortly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] We have another ten minutes to go. And did you know that while you were involved with the Security Council another incident took place in Miletici on 24th of April?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I understood later, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know, if anything, about this incident on the 24th of April?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I think this is the incident I got confused about, Your Honour, and I think this is an incident which we assessed to be carried out by the Mujahedin unit that was in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I'd like to refer you to tab 28, which is Exhibit P149, which is a milinfosum number 177, dated the 25th of April. I would refer you to page 4, which deals with the incident in Miletici. And more specifically, midway through paragraph 1 where it is stated that, "People in the area were keen to emphasise that the soldiers were extremist and not regular BiH troops." On that occasion and in the days following, did you have any reason to believe that this assessment that was made at that time was that Mujahedin had done this incident in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's what we believed, and this is the incident particularly that we felt was actually at the hands of -- of these Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, those Mujahedin, based on what you know from your time in Central Bosnia, would you say that those Mujahedin were part of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Most definitely not. They arrived in the area unbidden by the ABiH commanders, they made a damn nuisance of themselves and caused enormous problems, and they were not under command and control, to the very best of my knowledge. And I speak about this having had a source who I trust absolutely tell me a little about this group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you share the information you obtained from that source with us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I can. The information was that when the source met them on two occasions, they were grouped 15 to 20. The source met them to the north of Vitez once, to the east of Zenica on another occasion. The source said that one was French-speaking, extremely well dressed, quoting, "Dressed as a Parisian student. Very urbane, frighteningly cold." There were no BiH anywhere near the location that the source met these people. Indeed, they seemed to be operating in isolation and they were in both cases in civilian houses and in civilian dress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you share with us, Colonel, the identity of your source?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: No, I could not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you trust this source, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us when this conversation would have taken place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Around about this time. I don't know exactly when, but I met the source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you try to picture this incident in terms of -- or this conversation in where -- whether we say Ahmici is a reference point, is it before or after Ahmici, or is it later in time? Do you recall when this would have taken place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: On one or two occasions around the massacre of Ahmici, possibly before or possibly after. Around this period. I did not commit this to my diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going back quickly to the exchange of -- not the exchange, sorry, but the kidnapping of Totic. Do you think the 3rd Corps would have any advantage to gain from this event?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Quite the reverse. It was disaster that this event occurred. There would be no logic in actually kidnapping Totic. Everyone knew that the tension in Central Bosnia at the time was enormous. So whoever did it may well have done it deliberately to cause the fighting to start immediately, which of course it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you yourself involved in the events that followed with respect to what happened after this exchange?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: The exchange -- forgive me, but I must ask what you mean by --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, after the kidnapping. Sorry, my mistake. What happened after the kidnapping? Do you know what happened, if Totic was ever found?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I know -- you see, I left Bosnia unknowing. I assumed -- I made the assumption that Totic was dead. I couldn't see why -- I assumed it was Mujahedin - I was pretty certain of that - had taken him. I couldn't see why they would release him. So I was pretty certain that he was dead, and only recently, and I mean in the last few years, have I discovered, thank God, that he was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've got two more questions to ask you, and the first one is: Because we've been using some document called milinfosum which was produced by BritBat, would you provide -- could you provide the Trial Chamber with your assessment of the value of milinfosums.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I never wrote or, to the best of my knowledge, read a milinfosum. Every day, if I was in Vitez, I would hold a conference at 5.00. This conference was never and never did last longer than 30 minutes. At this conference I would listen to the intelligence, I would listen to the operational commanders underneath me, and I would make decisions. The milinfosum was a system, a rather tedious system, for reporting. I was concerned about what happened in the future, not reporting back. So maybe I was a bad commander in that respect, but I had a hell of a lot to do, and I felt my responsibility dictated that I spent most of my time in the field, not at my headquarters. So from my point of view, milinfosums were a good way of passing on general information. Now I've had a look at some of them, I'm somewhat perturbed by some of the assumptions and bad intelligence - it wasn't intelligence because it wasn't properly assessed - that actually went into those milinfosums that went to UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question to you, Colonel, is looking back at -- or first let me ask you: Did you have regular contacts with General Hadzihasanovic during your time in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I did, frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you comment on General Hadzihasanovic as a person and as a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. commander.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: As a person, he was calm, decent, honourable, and a gentleman. I liked being with him. We understood one another. As a commander, he was a man under extreme pressure with very few resources to call upon. He never ever was discourteous to me, and he was obviously, for most of the time I saw him, totally worn out, fatigued. But even so, tired as he was, he always treated me with utmost courtesy and never ever looked at his watch, which I would have done in his place. He always promised he would do his best to help. I have great respect and liking for the man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question to you, Colonel: Looking back on your own life, how would you qualify your time spent in Central Bosnia as part of the significant events which took place in your life?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that. Central Bosnia, to me, was probably -- do you say the high water mark of a military career? I knew I could never ever see anything or be part of anything like that again. I'm very, very concerned about what happens to Bosnia. I care very much about what happens, all the people. So I guess it's probably the high water mark of my military career.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am looking at Mr. Dixon now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I only have one or two questions, so I can do them before the break. Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Dixon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart, you have mentioned in your testimony today a number of commanders of the Bosnian army and the HVO at a higher level, at a corps level, that you dealt with during your time there, but you have also mentioned some of the brigades that they commanded. For example, you mentioned the 333rd Mountain Brigade. For the sake of completeness, could I confirm with you that you knew about a number of brigades in the 3rd Corps, including the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, but that this was a brigade that you knew very little about, and it was a brigade which was never brought to your attention for any particular reason; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct. There was only one brigade that I really investigated, and that was a brigade way up to the north which was a Bosnian Croat brigade, which was actually guarding a BiH position. But even the 333 Mountain Brigade, I only mentioned it today because it was on the document in front of me. To be quite honest, at my time, Your Honour, I knew so little about what was happening, structure and things, I really had to rely on personalities, and I would go to a personality rather than a brigade. So the answer to your question, Mr. Dixon, is I knew nothing really about 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you can recall, no issue ever arose in relation to the 7th Brigade during your time of duty there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: As per the 7th Brigade, no. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Stewart. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is half past 5.00. We're going to have the break now, but before the break could the Prosecution tell me, because we'll have only about one hour left after the break, in rough terms will the Prosecution need more than one hour? As the Defence has taken two hours and a quarter, and if the Prosecution needs more, the witness will have to be called back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. We need as much time as the Defence has used. Perhaps I'll be a little bit shorter, but I certainly need all of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is half past five. We're going to have the second regular break, and we will resume around five to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I give the floor to the Prosecution who will begin their cross-examination and will probably continue on tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Waespi

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good evening, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Good evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to go, in the remaining hour, over a few of the areas which you touched in your examination-in-chief. Let me first just clarify that I believe you told us you testified twice; in the Blaskic case, and that was on the 17th June, 1999, and in the Kordic and Cerkez case --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I believe I called it Santic. Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Kordic and Cerkez case, the 17th January 2000?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was almost five years ago, so I take it your memory at that time may have been slightly better than today, although I'm not doubting that you're still capable of remembering the essential things.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yeah. My memory gets worse each day I get older, but you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As everybody does. Now, the second point is your witness statement. I think you gave a witness statement in 1995 already to a gentleman called John E. Gerns from the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honours, if the witness statement could be shown to him. I've got a few copies. I'm not sure whether we need it but just to have the record clear. I have copies for everybody. Unfortunately, unstapled because I thought we wouldn't need it, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is being shown to refresh the witness's memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... might use it on one or two points later if he doesn't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have received this statement on the part of the witness, and we see no problem with my colleague using it to refresh the witness's memory if necessary, but we don't see why this statement should be distributed to everyone. If my colleague wishes to have it admitted, then we shall see, but this is a matter of principle. The statement, as such, is simply a collection of statements taken from the witness's diary. It's not the content. It is a matter of principle. If my colleague wishes to use it with the witness, no problem, but we don't see why it should be distributed to everyone in the way it has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue. The document will certainly not be admitted. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly to add to what Mr. Bourgon has said, and that is -- and I believe Mr. Waespi is going to do that, he should ask the witness the questions first and see if he does remember before he starts taking him through a witness statement. It's only, in our submission, if the witness cannot remember and he does think that he could recall the information by looking at his statement that he should then be taken to his statement. But if he can remember and give the evidence firsthand, that is the best evidence for Your Honours to have. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Prosecution has listened carefully to what has been said by the Defence, but I noted from the beginning that the witness doesn't even remember having given that statement. So this is an important point. It's better to go forward with questions, and then if he doesn't know the answer, then you can remind him that on such-and-such a day he said so-and-so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... at this point I don't intend yet to refresh his memory on that, but on the mere point whether he indeed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether you indeed remember having given the witness statement in July -- in June 1995. Do you remember that now, having seen the statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I do. In Belgium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: It was the "Gerns" that threw me. If it had been Dana who was questioning me, I would have understood, but you said "Gerns," and I couldn't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I had to see who was listed as the interviewer, and he was an investigator at that time, Mr. John Gerns. Your diary, just briefly to touch on that, you kept it, I understand, between the 28th of August 1992 until the 10th of May 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Just about. I didn't actually start on the 28th of August. It was written retrospectively because the general told me to start writing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to make that also clear, you told us you left on the 12th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: It was either the 11th or the 12th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your successor, who was that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Alistair Duncan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you told us you met him. He was present at a meeting already in February. Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it would, because he had two reconnaissances before he came in person to take over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks, Colonel. Now, let's go to substance and talk a little bit about these milinfosums. Can you tell us to whom they were addressed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: They were -- normally went to headquarters Bosnia-Herzegovina command, and they were sent nightly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of these milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: To keep the higher command aware of what was happening in my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it it was important that the information contained was as accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but I've already accepted that sometimes it was not as accurate as it should have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you can confirm that the people who drafted it - and perhaps you can tell us that later - they did whatever they could at that time to be as accurate as they could be?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, but they were junior officers normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what rank?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it probably could even have been a sergeant major. It could have been a lieutenant. At most it would have been a captain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said they would be given to higher command. How far up would those go?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: The responsibility is to go one level up. Then the higher command writes its own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they wouldn't have received the Ministry of Defence in London?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if Mr. Watters, who testified here, would have suggested that, that wouldn't be correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: No. I don't know the answer. Bryan Watters was my second in command. Normally they are sent only to the headquarters above who determine what actually should be passed up to the headquarters beyond it. But Bryan actually was in charge of the operations room when I was away and he may well have had instructions to send it simultaneously up the national chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I looked through some of them, and I think you also did because you said you -- you had some comments to make about them. I saw a couple of references like, I quote: "A normally reliable source," and then says something, or at another instance it says, "Unconfirmed and therefore not accurate." So that leads me to believe that indeed the -- your sergeants and up to the captain tried hard to make it as transparent as possible what they were reporting.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And I accept responsibility. They were meant to be done under my command and anything that happens under my command is my responsibility. So if they're inaccurate, it's inaccuracies by me, not by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you had every evening meetings in which you would receive information and discuss it with your, I guess, staff and immediate subordinates. What you discussed, would it be reflected generally in those milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Not necessarily. The purpose of the meeting every night was to -- for me to get an actual picture as to what's happening then and decide exactly what we were going to do in the next 24 hours. And I didn't actually have much time for milinfosums -- military information summaries at that time. I only had half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to your staff. You told us already that Major Watters, I believe he was your chief of staff and both your deputy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Correct. From about the end of February onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his predecessor was --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Tim Park.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you compare them, if you can? I mean it's sort of tricky to talk about an assessment of your subordinates, but can you tell us, you know, how good they were in completing their professional jobs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Tim was more of a -- was more operational, and Bryan was more detailed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Both were good officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would rely on them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I had no choice. I had to rely on them, and of course they were my officers. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you also told us that in the beginning, you were more concerned about the south of that area, Vakuf, Gornji, Donji Vakuf and that your second in command was looking towards the north. I believe it was an incident about Busovaca, and you said, you know, "My second in command knew what was happening." Was that the allocation of duties you had at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: It was de facto. The most urgent, pressing problem in my operational area was at Gornji Vakuf, and therefore it occupied my almost entire attention. But that didn't mean that the rest of the area could be ignored. So fundamentally, when I was away the operations room and the operations officer I had in that operations room, and Bryan Watters or Tim Park, would deal with that problem. But if there was a requirement for me to know about something, they would bring it to my attention, as they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was part of your immediate staff apart from your deputy commander/chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: My adjutant, who was -- dealt with discipline and routine administration; two operations officers, both captains, who maintained permanently a presence in the operations room; and of course various signalers and drivers who were with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the person, the adjutant who dealt with discipline. Did you have problems with discipline in your unit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: None whatsoever. Discipline meant that when someone committed an offence, something like losing an identity card, it was dealt with by him. I don't think my unit was out of control. But a good question, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I meant about out of control. How important is he in your -- was he in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: To be honest, the adjutant is probably the commanding officer's sounding board, the commanding officer's intimate staff officer, and he is probably the person to whom the commanding officer might talk quietly for advice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why he was also the person who dealt with these disciplinary aspects of it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you think that's very important to maintain that function.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's not just discipline he deals with, it's the running of the unit; when people leave, when people come. It's the sort of detailed management of a battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a brief thing. It's almost incidental. You told us you met a couple -- a number of times with Mr. Kordic and Dzemal Merdan, whom you praised. Now, do you recall that sometimes in 1992, I think it was in October, when you were in Novi Travnik Mr. Kordic called Mr. Merdan using his mobile phone? Do you remember that happening?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I was amazed. Because the British military told me they would not give me mobile phones because they wouldn't work. So once again, the British army triumphs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after there was even a fax exchange between Mr. Merdan and Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I was part of the fax, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the forces that were operating in the theatre. Now, you mentioned that you had a sort of a briefing, an introductory briefing, and you mentioned Mr. Colm Doyle, the head of the European Union mission to the BH. Now, you remember that, and I quote him, and I believe I quote your diary, what he told you, and I quote: "Most people in BiH are really good at twisting the truth. All are quite prepared to attack their own people and blame it on someone else." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: That's exactly what he said. I remember it because I wrote it down in my diary, and it was said in Zagreb. And I think Colm Doyle was the political assistant to Lord Owen or something like that. He was the -- you see, at this time, Your Honours, I was trying to get as much information as I could, and this was information that I hadn't got, so I wrote it down. That's exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it helpful for you in your further dealings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it gave me an idea of what was happening. And I just took it as I knew nothing. I wrote it down and I considered it. I didn't know any better. This was a source of information. The Ministry of Defence in London hadn't given me such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe he was Irish, Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, how many times in your dealings with these warring factions, their commanders, have you -- politicians, have you heard the excuse elements allegedly perpetrating something were out of control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Actually, no, not very many times. I'm now using my mind. I used to say they were out of control. For example, when my driver, my escort driver was killed, shot through the head on the 13th of January, it was in my opinion done by soldier of the Bosnian BiH. A good shot, if that's not too foul to say. But I believed it was the BiH soldier that did it. And I also had incidents with the HVO. I don't believe that they were under instructions from their chain of command to engage the United Nations. In fact, I am pretty sure they weren't. And that includes the HVO. So I used to put it down to lack of control, out of control soldiers, such as on the 13th of January. I don't think commanders necessarily would admit to me that their forces were out of control. I would just think they might have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you mentioned Mr. Kordic in relation to Ahmici. Do you remember - you might have talked about that - that after Ahmici occurred you went to him and put to him what has happened in Ahmici in your view, and do you remember that he told you it might have been the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yeah. That's what he said. He said that it was a long-range patrol of the Bosnian Serb army that might have done the -- and I just laughed. I said a very long-range patrol that went right past your checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't believe him.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: No, of course I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in line with what Doyle had told you at the outset of your mission?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes; Doyle's information was wrong. I mean, he was a political officer in a political place picking up information from I don't know where. But Doyle was doing the best he could, and he was giving us a briefing after he'd ceased to be in that position, and that's fine. I mean, a lot of briefings are wrong. And to say there were lots of Mujahedin, I didn't see evidence of that. And one of the things I learnt quickly in Bosnia was if we don't actually see it ourselves, don't trust it. So that's one of the principles I tried to apply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on this point, Mr. Kordic was wrong, or did you believe Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: On what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the Serbs were responsible for Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: No. I repeat: He was totally wrong. He was not -- the Bosnian Serb army was not responsible for Ahmici. That was done by units of the HVO, special or otherwise. That's my absolute belief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us again what Mr. Kordic's position was.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Very good point. That's exactly what most people around this courtroom would like to know, to be honest. I never really ascertained what Dario Kordic's position was. Was he in charge of Blaskic or was he not? The International Criminal Tribunal probably ascertained that but I wasn't good enough to read through all the transcripts. Kordic seemed to be the political commander and Blaskic seemed to be the military commander. Who was in charge of who was something of quite big importance to us, but at the stage when - excuse me - when Busovaca was -- had checkpoints at either end, Kordic was actually the commander in the PTT building at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's fair to say that Kordic was one of the higher personalities in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he lied to you about who committed Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I believe he lied, yes, because the massacre of Ahmici, we all know, was carried out not by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's turn briefly to Mr. Hadzihasanovic. Were there also occasionally moments that he appeared to -- not to be quite truthful in what he was saying to you? Do you remember any -- any incident?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I'm thinking. I don't think -- I don't think -- I don't think there were. I mean -- you know, I would take complaints to General Hadzihasanovic, and I would explain them, and he would say, "I will do my best to sort them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know there might be incidents in your subordinates' milinfosums which reflect that Hadzihasanovic wasn't speaking the truth or was less than accurate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: It's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were quite enthusiastic about Mr. Hadzihasanovic today. Do you remember what you told about him in the Kordic trial?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: That he was a bit more sly than Merdan; something like that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read out to you what you said.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that is, as I mentioned before, a quote from his testimony in the Kordic, Cerkez trial, 18 January 2000, on pages 15521 and 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just read out what you were asked. I believe it was Mr. Nice. He asked you: "The last point, Hadzihasanovic you mentioned as one of those willing to cooperate, I think. Just in a word or phrase, he's a reliable, unreliable, honourable, dishonourable, whatever it is man, Hadzihasanovic." And your answer: "I don't know. The one person I trusted was Merdan, in the same way as I trusted Blaskic." Question: "So you can't comment on Hadzihasanovic." Answer: "Well, I don't know. I mean, saw a lot of him. He seemed to be okay but I didn't feel particularly sympatico with him." Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you stand by that today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I've given a lot of thought since then about Hadzihasanovic, of course, because this is a trial. And yes, I said that, and yes I've thought it through a great deal since then, and actually, I have a slightly different view. I've tried to find out where I could actually justify any kind of sneakiness by Hadzihasanovic. I've been through my diaries, I've looked, and I haven't seen anything. So this is very important for me to get this sorted out, and that's my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What in fact triggered your review of your opinion about Mr. Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: When I discovered that he was being brought to trial, which I think is a disgrace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why do you think it's a disgrace?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Because he had -- if the charge is that he was in control of Mujahedin units, he wasn't, and it's unfair to have that charge brought against him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe you told us about the information, and we'll come to that in a moment. Control over roads. I believe my colleague Residovic once asked a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness that who controls the roads in Bosnia controls Bosnia. Would you agree with her assessment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Up to a point, yes. But we didn't necessarily control roads. We controlled areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no objection to my colleague citing what the witness may have said, but to have an opinion, I don't think this should be submitted to the witness in the form of a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not the opinion of the attorney but the opinion of the witness who said that those who controlled the roads controlled Bosnia and Herzegovina. I remember very well what the witness said in answer to a question, a leading question one might say. But perhaps you should quote the page when the witness gave this answer to see whether this was an answer to a leading question on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm quite sure, Mr. President, that it was one of these leading questions by Ms. Residovic perhaps justified in the moment. I will try to find it overnight, and I can tell you exactly where it comes from tomorrow. I won't go into that subject right now, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to this sensitive subject of control over the Mujahedin. Let's start again with your diary, and let's have a look at the entry of the 21st -- the 25th September. I believe it's the same day you had that conversation with Mr. Doyle, and it may have been the same event in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that's a new document, although the Defence has relied on it. The witness obviously talked about his diary. It doesn't need to be an exhibit. I just would like to ask him to read out what concerned that specific mentioning of the forces that operated in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objection, Mr. President, for the witness to use his diary which he wrote himself to answer the question. If the Prosecution wishes to tender the diary, then the position may be different, but otherwise we have no objection that he consult his diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then the Prosecution may use this diary as they see fit, quoting the whole paragraph that he may have written or asking him to read it out himself, whichever you prefer. But find the most efficient solution and which will save time. As you know, time is very precious.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you're the native English speaker, perhaps you could tell us, on the page where you discuss this introduction meeting of some Friday, 25th of September, I believe a Major Jonathan Reely or Reilly, Ops Officer European Community Monitoring Mission, talks about the different forces that operate in the area, and perhaps you can read out what he says just after his name about the different warring factions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Of course. "Major Jonathan Reilly, of the Royal West Fusiliers, the Ops Officer of the European Community Monitoring Mission, started: It seems that the Bosnian Serbs, the TDF, have about 70.000 troops deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The land link between Serbia proper and their forces in the west of BiH is of the greatest strategic importance. The Croatian Defence Council, the HVO, is weaker with about 45 to 50.000 troops. The HVO are trying to close this strategic corridor. Finally, the Bosnian territorial defence force, TDF, consists of about 50.000 South Slav Muslims which are now being reinforced by Mujahedin from Islamic fundamentalist countries."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's what you were told at that time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I was told at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any doubt to mistrust this piece of information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: None whatsoever, as I knew nothing. That's why I wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move on to the time when you actually got operational in Bosnia. And in your various contacts with units and commanders, perhaps Mujahedin. Have you ever had contacts with Mujahedin yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I've seen them. I've got close to them. I've gone through sort of a roadblock controlled by them. Did I have contacts with them? Apart from indicating "Get out of the way," no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the location of that roadblock or those roadblocks where you might have encountered them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: I particularly remember at the top of the mountain road to Zenica from Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So between Dubravica and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the middle, basically?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: At the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I might try to give you a map tomorrow so you can tell us. Can you tell us what happened at that roadblock or checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't so much of a roadblock, it was just a group of them on the road, and they were trying to sort of -- it was a sort of standoff, really, and I wanted to go through and they were blocking, and eventually I said, "Get out of the way," and they went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they look like? What were they wearing, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: Most of them were wearing civilian clothes. But they were armed. And they didn't look like Bosnians. And that was really the closest I came to the Mujahedin groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: No. I couldn't, really. I was on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Have you ever heard that Iranian instructors were training the Bosnian forces, Bosnian forces under the command and control of Mr. Hadzihasanovic? Have you ever heard about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT STEWART
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no, although my source suggested that some of them were Iranian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps that would be a good moment to give Your Honours the list of proposed exhibits or documents I would like to discuss with this witness. And if the witness could be provided with just one tab out of the documents, and that would be tab 5, Prosecution Exhibit P533. So don't show the witness the whole document but please rip it apart before so he only sees that specific exhibit. It's tab number 5, P433. And that's an existing exhibit which is in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I rise at this point simply to point out that, yes, this document is an exhibit, but it is a document that is purportedly one that comes from the 7th Brigade. So it's an internal document of that brigade. And of course the witness must have a look at the document, but it's highly unlikely, given his testimony earlier, that he would have seen this document. He said he never had access to these kinds of documents. And I just wish to put a marker down now that if in the cross-examination my learned friend is going to seek to show the witness a number of documents that he hasn't seen, in our submission it's going to be a pointless exercise because he's not going to be able to give any information about the content of these documents. Some of these have been shown to witnesses before and they have been able to comment on them, and certainly 7th Brigade documents will be shown to witnesses in the case for Mr. Kubura, witnesses from the 7th Brigade who will be able to assist Your Honours with the content of these documents, and in our submission that would be the appropriate time for these to be looked at and not through a witness who never had access to them. Thank you Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In all due respect to Mr. Dixon, this witness had commented on a number of documents he has never seen of Mr. Hadzihasanovic and was asked to comment, and I quote: "What is Hadzihasanovic doing with this document?" That was the only connection, allegedly, he had. And this witness now has said, yes, he has heard about Iranian instructors, and I would like to show him the document and see whether that corroborates the information his source has given him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment. I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Bourgon, but in the French translation I heard Iranian instructors, which he himself mentioned. I never heard from the witness any spontaneous mention of Iranian instructors. It was you who told him that there were Iranian instructors. But maybe the witness can clarify before Mr. Bourgon takes the floor. Colonel, there's a small problem. Reference was made to Iranian instructors. Was it you who spontaneously mentioned Iranian instructors or were you answering a question, a leading question, concerning the possibility that the 3rd Corps had Iranian instructors? Could you clarify this point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- I said that my source told me that the source thought there were Iranian members in the Mujahedin group that the source met. I didn't say anything about instructors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that your source said that among the Mujahedin there may have been Iranians, but there was never any mention of instructors. That was my impression too. The Prosecution. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness could be shown -- if the witness could be shown the document, and perhaps it refreshes his recollection what he -- what he has heard from this source --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, was this on this point that you -- was it on this point that you wanted to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The question is the following: Indeed during the examination-in-chief, the witness did use documents coming from the 3rd Corps, but before showing those documents to the witness, I asked him if I showed him documents from the 3rd Corps but not from any sub-unit referring to an event that he was involved in, would this witness be able to comment on that document, and that is quite a different matter than to take a document following certain answers of the witness. He already said that he knew nothing about the 7th Brigade, and he was shown a document apparently to refresh his memory. But I think these are two different approaches, and it is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What will you say now on the part of the Prosecution? The debate is very simple. The Defence tell us that they did show certain documents to the witness but solely from the 3rd Corps and not of any unit under the command of the 3rd Corps, and that through the question that you put, you wanted, by showing him the document, you wanted him to confirm that there were Iranian instructors, whereas he himself never mentioned the existence of Iranian instructors. Is that how you wish to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Keep also in mind that this witness volunteered the information that the Mujahedin, in assessment -- in his assessment, were not under the control of the 3rd Corps or the ABiH, I don't know. And here we have a document which shows that Iranian instructors indeed trained units of the 3rd Corps, and I would like to see his comment whether he has anything to say about that, that it suggests that there is more connection between Mujahedin and the 3rd Corps than he has seen so far. It just shows how much knowledge there is on his part to make his assessment. That's my only point.
